ENT Clinical Note – Telehealth Visit

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • “Blinding” headache for 3 days; no clear food, medication, or environmental trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Sudden onset on waking 3 days ago → persistent and daily.  
  • Baseline intensity 8/10, decreases to ~5/10 with ibuprofen but never fully resolves.
- ENT-related symptoms:
  • Throat: no swelling/closure sensation, no voice change, no dysphagia/odynophagia, no drooling.  
  • Nasal/ocular: photophobia; no congestion, rhinorrhea, epistaxis, or change in smell/taste.  
  • Respiratory/airway: no stridor, noisy breathing, or dyspnea.  
  • Swelling: none of lips, tongue, uvula, or face.  
  • Otologic/neck: no ear pain, hearing changes, or neck pain/swelling.
- Associated neurologic/other features: transient “shooting lights” in vision; mild nausea but no vomiting; no focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty; able to sleep, headache not waking patient.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Prior brief, mild headaches resolving with ibuprofen; first prolonged episode.  
  • No previous ED visits or injection therapy.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies: none reported.  
  • Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand not documented) – 1 tablet daily (exact dose/strength not documented).  
  • Ibuprofen PRN (dose/frequency not documented). No other regular or rescue meds.
- Social context: Lives alone; works from home; non-smoker; drinks ~3 alcoholic drinks once weekly; no recent travel.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: none reported/seen via video.
- Airway/breathing: normal speech; no audible stridor or respiratory distress.
- Mental status: alert and coherent throughout call.
- Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded (telehealth; in-person exam pending).
- Accompaniment: patient alone during call.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: New severe unilateral headache with photophobia and visual aura – most consistent with migraine with aura; however, must rule out secondary causes.
  • Evidence: right-predominant pain, visual phenomena, photophobia, family history of migraine, partial NSAID response, absence of fever or neurologic deficit.
- DDx (aligned with transcript and DDx engine):
  1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood; classic features and family history.
  2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Medium likelihood; risk factor (estrogen OCP) and persistent severe headache; no focal deficits (opposing evidence).
  3. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – Medium-low likelihood; young woman with visual disturbance; lacks papilledema or positional pattern (opposing evidence).
- No material conflicts between transcript and DDx.

Plan:
- Medications:
  • Prescribed a stronger NSAID (name/dose to be provided on prescription) to take with food, PLUS regular paracetamol as needed.  
  • Continue current OCP for now; advise possible change if migraine with aura confirmed.
- Follow-up / investigations:
  • Book urgent in-person appointment for full neurologic and ENT-focused examination, including fundoscopy, optic disc assessment, and blood pressure check.  
  • Consider neuro-imaging or urgent referral if exam reveals papilledema, focal deficit, or if headache persists >72 h despite therapy.
- Patient instructions:
  • Use prescribed analgesics as directed; maintain hydration and rest in low-light environment.  
  • Seek emergency care (A&E/EMS) immediately for: sudden escalation of pain, vomiting, visual loss, weakness, speech change, confusion, fever, neck stiffness, or any airway/ENT symptoms (stridor, throat swelling, dysphagia).  
  • Contact clinic if symptoms improve and appointment needs adjusting.
- Education:
  • Reviewed potential relationship between estrogen OCP and migraines; discussed that pill may need to be changed after evaluation.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but expected elements: vital signs, detailed neuro & ENT physical exam (otoscopy, nasal cavity, oropharynx, neck palpation), fundoscopy findings, exact medication doses, full allergy list, review of auto-injector/anaphylaxis plan (not relevant but commonly checked), detailed past medical history.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional inaudible portions (patient name, OCP brand) without clinical relevance.
